# 4 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Eleazar's First Confrontation with Antiochus

---

**1** When the tyrant Antiochus found that his efforts were being resisted and that the people clung to their ancestral law, he commanded his soldiers to force every Hebrew to eat food that was contrary to the law.

**2** Anyone who refused was to be tortured to death.

**3** Among the many who were brought in was Eleazar, well known by the king's attendants — a priest by descent, well trained in the law, advanced in age, and distinguished by his reputation as a philosopher.

**4** Antiochus saw him and addressed him as follows:

**5** Before I proceed to torment you, old man, I will offer you some advice: taste the meat and save your life.

**6** I have respect for your age and your white hair, though I find it difficult to regard an intelligent man as truly wise when he holds such views.

**7** For what compels you to observe this Jewish religion that deprives you of the natural pleasures of life?

**8** I believe it is a mistake to refuse the enjoyment of pleasures that involve no harm.

**9** I think you would act more wisely if you adopted the customs of those of your people who have already conformed to our way of life.

**10** I therefore urge you to abandon your old prejudices and take up a new and more enlightened point of view.

**11** Have compassion on your age; honor your venerable years.

**12** Consider: if there is some divine guardian of your religion, he will surely forgive a transgression committed under compulsion.

**13** But if you persist in your old-fashioned scruples, you will be put to death as an example to others.

**14** When Antiochus had said this, he instructed his guards to bring in the instruments of torture.

**15** Eleazar looked at them without flinching, raised his eyes toward heaven, and asked for permission to speak.

**16** Permission being granted, he addressed the assembly in these words:

**17** Antiochus, we who have been convinced to govern our lives by the divine law do not believe any compulsion to be stronger than obedience to that law.

**18** We consider it right in no respect to transgress it.

**19** Even if our law were, as you suppose, not truly divine, and we had held it to be divine through error — even then it would not be fitting for us to abandon our reputation for godliness.

**20** Do not suppose it is a small thing if we eat the forbidden food.

**21** For to transgress the law in small things or in great things is equally grave, since in both cases alike the law is equally disregarded.

**22** You make sport of our philosophy as if we lived in a manner unworthy of it. But in fact our law has taught us self-control, so that we master every pleasure and desire; it has instructed us in fortitude, so that we endure every pain with courage; it has trained us in justice, so that in all our affairs we treat others fairly; and it has schooled us in godliness, so that we worship the one God in the manner that is truly worthy of his majesty.

**23** Therefore we do not eat defiling food.

**24** Since we believe that the law was given by God, we also know that the God who created the world, being moved by compassion, has granted us what is suited to our souls and has forbidden what is harmful to them.

**25** The tyrant, as though the words had been spoken by someone entirely without reason, dismissed them with contempt and ordered the application of the tortures.
